extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and students of poetics/literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating Greek tragedy and epic poetry, covering plot construction, diction, metre, use of episodes, chorus, and how to meet or answer criticisms about improbability or impossibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action (single action with beginning, middle, and end)
rubrics_metrics.description: The construction of its stories should clearly be like that in a drama; they should be based on a single action, one that is a complete whole in itself, with a beginning, middle, and end, so as to enable the work to produce its own proper pleasure with all the organic unity of a living creature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic and tragic plots must concentrate on one unified action rather than a succession of disconnected events; Homer succeeds by singling out a section of a larger story and treating other incidents as episodes (e.g., Catalogue of Ships). Avoid treating an entire multi-thread epic (e.g., whole Iliad) as a single dramatic plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplify story to a universal/core form before adding episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: His story ... he should first simplify and reduce to a universal form, before proceeding to lengthen it out by the insertion of episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce the plot to its universal element (example: Iphigenia framed as 'maiden offered in sacrifice and spirited away, later brother recognized and saved') and only then add appropriate accessory incidents or episodes to flesh it out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness and brevity of episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: One must mind, however, that the episodes are appropriate, like the fit of madness in Orestes, which led to his arrest, and the purifying, which brought about his salvation. In plays, then, the episodes are short; in epic poetry they serve to lengthen out the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Episodes should advance or be coherent with the main action; in drama they should be brief and relevant; irrelevant or ill-fitting episodes weaken the plot's unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure: Complication and Denouement around the turning point
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy is in part Complication and in part Denouement; by Complication I mean all from the beginning of the story to the point just before the change in the hero's fortunes; by Denouement, all from the beginning of the change to the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging sameness/difference of plots compare their Complication and Denouement. Both parts must be well constructed; many dramatists succeed in Complication but fail in Denouement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species of tragedy and combining elements
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four distinct species of Tragedy: first, the complex (all Peripety and Discovery); second, the Tragedy of suffering; third, the Tragedy of character; fourth, that of 'Spectacle'. The poet's aim should be to combine every element of interest, if possible, or else the more important and the major part of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to include peripety (reversal), discovery, character development, suffering, and spectacle as appropriate; if you cannot include all, prioritize the major elements that will produce the intended effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dramatizing an epic's entire multi-part story
rubrics_metrics.description: One should also remember ... not write a tragedy on an epic body of incident (i.e. one with a plurality of stories in it), by attempting to dramatize, for instance, the entire story of the Iliad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a part of a large epic to dramatize; attempting the whole leads to overlong, unfocused drama and usually failure on stage (historical examples: unsuccessful complete dramatizations of Ilium).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus should be an integral actor in the action
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus too should be regarded as one of the actors; it should be an integral part of the whole, and take a share in the action—that which it has in Sophocles rather than in Euripides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choric songs and interventions ought to relate to and participate in the plot; purely intercalary songs that do not connect to the action are a later (less desirable) practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought must be shown through language and action
rubrics_metrics.description: The Thought of the personages is shown in everything to be effected by their language—i.e. every effort to prove or disprove, to arouse emotion (pity, fear, anger, and the like), or to maximize or minimize things. ... their mental procedure must be on the same lines in their actions likewise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character's reasoning and intentions should be evident through their speech and deeds; speech explains where action cannot, while action must itself be expressive without extraneous explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction taxonomy and awareness of linguistic elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The Diction viewed as a whole is made up of the following parts: the Letter (or ultimate element), the Syllable, the Conjunction, the Article, the Noun, the Verb, the Case, and the Speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand basic linguistic building blocks and their functions (phonology, word-formation, syntax) since diction choices affect meter, clarity, and poetic effect; detailed metric matters are for metricians but awareness aids composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction should be clear and not mean (balance ordinary and unfamiliar words)
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfection of Diction is for it to be at once clear and not mean. The clearest indeed is that made up of the ordinary words for things, but it is mean. On the other hand the Diction becomes distinguished and non-prosaic by the use of unfamiliar terms ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mix ordinary words (for clarity) with strange words, metaphors, and ornamental forms (for distinction). Overuse of unfamiliar forms produces riddles or barbarisms; moderation is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use metaphors with mastery—sign of genius
rubrics_metrics.description: But the greatest thing by far is to be a master of metaphor. It is the one thing that cannot be learnt from others; and it is also a sign of genius, since a good metaphor implies an intuitive perception of the similarity in dissimilars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate original, apt metaphors; they elevate diction beyond mere strange words. Study types of metaphor (genus↔species, species↔genus, species↔species, analogy) and qualified metaphors (adding the related term or negative qualification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper use of poetic licences (strange, coined, lengthened, curtailed, altered words)
rubrics_metrics.description: A coined word is a name which, being quite unknown among a people, is given by the poet himself ... A word is said to be lengthened out ... It is said to be curtailed ... It is an altered word ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such licences give non-prosaic character yet must be used sparingly; test by substituting ordinary words into a line to see if the poetic effect relies on the licence or obscures meaning. Excess invites ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match diction types to genre and metre
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds are most in place in the dithyramb, strange words in heroic, and metaphors in iambic poetry. Heroic poetry, indeed, may avail itself of them all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose word-forms appropriate to the poetic species and metre: heroic metre tolerates strange words and elaborate diction; iambic (modelled on spoken language) prefers ordinary words, metaphors, ornamental equivalents allowable in oration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic length and metre constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: As to its length, the limit already suggested will suffice: it must be possible for the beginning and end of the work to be taken in in one view ... As for its metre, the heroic has been assigned it from experience; ... the heroic is the gravest and weightiest of metres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic should be long enough for grandeur and episodes but not so long the whole cannot be grasped at once; use heroic metre for long narrative; avoid medleys of metres for an epic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial intrusion in epic should be minimal
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should say very little in propria persona, as he is no imitator when doing that. Homer after a brief preface brings in forthwith a man, a woman, or some other Character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let characters and action speak for the poem; avoid excessive authorial commentary which breaks imitation and reduces poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marvellous and improbable: genre-appropriate tolerance
rubrics_metrics.description: The marvellous is certainly required in Tragedy. The Epic, however, affords more opening for the improbable, the chief factor in the marvellous, because in it the agents are not visibly before one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy may legitimately invoke the marvellous for effect; epic can accommodate improbable incidents more easily. However, improbable incidents should be concealed or justified by other excellence; avoid outright absurdities within the work's core action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer a likely impossibility to an unconvincing possibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A likely impossibility is always preferable to an unconvincing possibility. The story should never be made up of improbable incidents; there should be nothing of the sort in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When improbable elements are necessary, make them seem likely or place them outside the main action (as antecedent assumptions) rather than rely on implausible developments within the plot. Conceal improbabilities with other excellences of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elaborate diction only where no action, character, or thought is revealed
rubrics_metrics.description: Elaborate Diction, however, is required only in places where there is no action, and no Character or Thought to be revealed. Where there is Character or Thought, on the other hand, an over-ornate Diction tends to obscure them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve ornate language for descriptive or digressive passages; when revealing character or thought, prefer clarity and directness to avoid obscuring psychological or ethical content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish poetic errors vs accidental/technical errors
rubrics_metrics.description: There is not the same kind of correctness in poetry as in politics, or indeed any other art. There is ... two kinds of error, the one directly, the other only accidentally connected with the art. If the poet meant to describe the thing correctly, and failed through lack of power of expression, his art itself is at fault. But if it was through his having meant to describe it in some incorrect way ... then the error is not in the essentials of the poetic art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing faults, determine whether an apparent inaccuracy is intentional (serving poetic ends) or a real failure of expression/knowledge; judge less harshly when inaccuracies are used to improve the poetic effect and are not gratuitous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify impossibilities, improbabilities, contradictions by poetic ends, opinion, or custom
rubrics_metrics.description: One has to justify (1) the Impossible by reference to the requirements of poetry, or to the better, or to opinion. (2) The Improbable one has to justify either by showing it to be in accordance with opinion, or by urging that at times it is not improbable. (3) The contradictions found in the poet's language one should first test ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defenses include: appeal to the aims of poetry (astonishment, effect), appeal to audience opinion/convention, appeal to occasional probability, linguistic re-interpretation (metaphor, punctuation, equivocal terms), or technical explanation. Use these methods to answer critics' objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five kinds of criticisable faults and how to address them
rubrics_metrics.description: The objections ... start with faults of five kinds: the allegation is always that something is either (1) impossible, (2) improbable, (3) corrupting, (4) contradictory, or (5) against technical correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When responding to criticism, identify which of the five categories the objection falls into and respond via the appropriate head(s) of justification (poetic necessity, opinion, linguistic reading, technical correction, or moral/contextual defence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary improbability or depravity of character
rubrics_metrics.description: But there is no possible apology for improbability of Plot or depravity of character, when they are not necessary and no use is made of them, like the improbability in the appearance of Aegeus in Medea and the baseness of Menelaus in Orestes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not introduce implausible plot turns or morally corrupt character traits unless they are necessary to the plot and serve a useful artistic purpose; gratuitous faults undermine the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use linguistic and interpretive techniques to resolve apparent faults
rubrics_metrics.description: Other criticisms one must meet by considering the language of the poet: (1) by the assumption of a strange word ... (2) Other expressions in Homer may be explained as metaphorical; (3) A change in the mode of reading a word will solve the difficulty; (4) by another punctuation; (5) by the assumption of an equivocal term; (6) by an appeal to the custom of language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When critics point to textual or conceptual faults, consider reinterpretation tactics: assume dialectal/strange-word senses, read metaphors, alter reading/punctuation, exploit equivocal words, or appeal to linguistic/customary usage before condemning the poet.
